disclaimer: This is a source-backed evidence checklist, not a replacement for a published taxonomic key. A checked item records that the structure is visible; it does not by itself confirm a genus.

fallback.title: Evidence checklist before using a genus key

steps.title: Whole specimen
steps.inspect: Take a sharp dorsal and lateral photograph with the entire body, wing tips and legs visible.
steps.why: Body proportions, colour pattern and major setae are lost when appendages are cropped.

steps.title: Head and antenna
steps.inspect: Add a close lateral or oblique view of the antenna, eyes, face, palps and mouthparts.
steps.why: Many genus keys depend on antennal segments, eye shape and facial characters.

steps.title: Wing
steps.inspect: Photograph one wing flat and in focus, including its base, veins, membrane and margin.
steps.why: Venation, setulae and the calypter/squama frequently separate genera.

steps.title: Legs
steps.inspect: Show tibial spurs, apical combs and the last tarsal segments at high magnification.
steps.why: Leg armature and pulvilli can be diagnostic but are rarely resolved in a habitus image.

steps.title: Terminalia
steps.inspect: If permitted, add a correctly oriented macro or microscope image of the terminalia.
steps.why: For many small Diptera, a reliable species decision requires sex-specific terminalia.

stop_rules: Stop at family or genus when a required structure is hidden, blurred or outside the frame.
Do not promote a species suggestion solely because its model score is high.
Use a key whose sex, life stage and geographic scope match the specimen.

Chironomidae.title: Adult Chironomidae: what to inspect before comparing genera
Chironomidae.scope: adult specimen; male and female keys are not interchangeable

steps.title: 1. Confirm life stage and sex
steps.inspect: Record adult/larva/pupa and male/female. In an adult, photograph the antenna and terminalia clearly.
steps.why: The major Chironomidae keys are stage- and often sex-specific; adult male terminalia carry much of the genus/species evidence.

steps.title: 2. Head and antenna
steps.inspect: Capture the antennal flagellum and plume, eyes in dorsal view, palps and mouthparts. Do not infer antennal ratios from a blurred oblique image.
steps.why: Antenna, eye extension and palpal characters are repeatedly used in adult genus diagnoses.

steps.title: 3. Wing and squama
steps.inspect: Flatten one wing. Resolve membrane macrotrichia, vein setation and course, costa ending, anal lobe, and whether the squama bears a fringe.
steps.why: These characters help route an adult through subfamily and genus keys.

steps.title: 4. Thoracic setae
steps.inspect: Make a dorsal close-up showing acrostichal, dorsocentral and prealar setae and the scutellum.
steps.why: Setal arrangement is useful, but usually invisible in a whole-body phone photograph.

steps.title: 5. Tibiae and tarsi
steps.inspect: Photograph the apices of all tibiae, including combs/spurs, and the tarsal claws, pulvilli and empodium.
steps.why: Leg-armature states distinguish several adult lineages and genera.

steps.title: 6. Male hypopygium
steps.inspect: For a male, obtain a correctly oriented microscope image or slide preparation showing gonostylus, gonocoxite and volsellae.
steps.why: Many adult male genera and most difficult species cannot be tested responsibly without hypopygial characters.

steps.title: 7. Add another life stage or DNA when possible
steps.inspect: Preserve pupal exuviae/larva with the adult, or obtain a COI barcode for a voucher.
steps.why: Associated stages and DNA can resolve cases in which adult habitus is convergent or species limits are cryptic.

stop_rules: If sex or life stage is unknown, do not enter a sex- or stage-specific key.
If wing, tibial apex or terminalia cannot be inspected, treat the model genus as a hypothesis only.
For a species claim, require the characters stated in the applicable revision; many Chironomidae are not identifiable from a single habitus photo.
When morphology and the image model disagree, retain both candidates and request specialist or DNA evidence.
